sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. In 400B-token pretraining, U-MoLT outperforms OLMo3 across 700M/1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, achieving 1.7x validation cross-entropy (CE) token efficiency at 700M while improving 3B MoE 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. In 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation lowers CE on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4x mean token efficiency. At inference, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 matches non-looped OLMo3 latency at 996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms on S-size (~113M) models. Code is available at https://github.com/hustvl/MoLT

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Model architecture design is fundamentally tradeoff between expressivity and efficiency. Recent frontier architectures have largely advanced this tradeoff through sparser computation, linear attention, and richer cross-layer connectivity [14, 27, 28, 55, 65, 70]. More recently, looped Transformers have risen to the forefront of architecture design and achieved remarkable success [9, 15, 19, 57, 69, 71]. This stems from reusing parameters across repeated loops for stronger expressivity, though at the cost of efficiency. Building on this paradigm, we pursue next-generation foundation model architectures that combine stronger expressivity with high computational efficiency. Achieving this requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as Transformer loops? The standard answer is loop residual, which passes each loops output directly into the next loop. This choice bottlenecks both expressivity and efficiency. Repeatedly compressing computation into single residual stream causes information dilution across layers and loops, leading to representational degradation. Moreover, each token depends on its own preceding-loop output, forcing inference to run every loop sequentially. Instead of relying solely on residual stream, our answer is to pass computed keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) lets each layer jointly attend to KV from different depths and loops  (Fig. 1)  . Under loop residual, MoLT-R keeps the residual stream across loops for maximum expressivity. MoLA directly reads current-loop and preceding-loop local KV at the same token position, mitigating information dilution through selective reuse. When decoding 2 efficiency is the priority, keeping the residual stream still requires sequential loop execution. To remove this bottleneck, we ask whether each loop can start afresh and rely purely on KV memory. This motivates the loop KV paradigm, in which each loop restarts from embeddings. In MoLT-KV, MoLA jointly reads memory KV projected from the preceding loops outputs at strictly earlier positions and currentloop local KV at the current token. We introduce loop forcing to train this paradigm, supervising every loop while training each feedback loop in parallel from preceding-loop memory KV rather than sequentially decoded prefixes. Because each loop restarts from embeddings and reads memory KV only from earlier positions, token no longer depends on its own preceding-loop output. This unlocks Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding, where each new token skips the preceding loops and traverses the shared stack once. It reads cached prefix memory KV alongside current-loop local KV and appends new memory KV for subsequent tokens, extending looped computation beyond the training loop horizon. For fast prompt processing, MoL-Hybrid decoding further pairs parallel fixed-loop prefill with MoL decoding. MoLT-KV brings single-traversal decoding to plain stack while looping all layers. To further lower prefill cost and balance efficiency with quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), inspired by encoder-source reuse in YOCO, Universal YOCO, and DeepSeeks CED architecture [14, 55, 56]. U-MoLT separates memory construction from prediction readout. It pairs loop KV MoLT Encoder with cross-only MoLT Decoder that reads the normalized encoder output through independent per-layer decoder KV projections. The decoder stays outside the encoder loop and does not depend on decoder states at earlier positions. At inference, U-MoLT therefore skips decoder traversals at intermediate loops and non-final prompt positions without changing the next-token prediction. Across scales and architectures, MoLT pushes the expressivity and efficiency frontier of looped models  (Fig. 2)  . In 400B-token from-scratch pretraining against OLMo3, U-MoLT improves mean validation perplexity and downstream accuracy on 700M dense, 1.5B dense, and 3B mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. At 700M scale, MoLT-R and U-MoLT raise 10-task accuracy by 2.6 and 2.5 percentage points, and U-MoLT matches OLMo3s final mean validation cross-entropy with 1.7 token efficiency. On 3B MoE models with 660M active parameters, U-MoLT lowers 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and raises 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. Beyond pretraining from scratch, we validate cross-architecture continued pretraining on Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, where U-MoLT reduces validation cross-entropy on all 11 domains over the matched 100B-token baseline with 1.4 mean token efficiency. At inference, MoL-Hybrid decoding eliminates the latency penalty of fixed-loop decoding while preserving prediction quality. On S-size (113M) models with 4,096-token prompts and 64 decoding steps, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 runs in 996.6 ms, matching non-looped OLMo3 at 1,000.6 ms. The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: We address the expressivityefficiency bottleneck of looped Transformers and propose new family of model architectures, MoLT, spanning MoLT-R (loop residual), MoLT-KV (loop KV), and U-MoLT. Through MoLA, MoLT passes computed KV as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops, while U-MoLT separates memory construction from prediction readout. We introduce loop-forcing training and MoL decoding. To our knowledge, MoL decoding is the first single-traversal scheme that runs looped Transformers beyond the training loop horizon. By reading cached prefix memory KV alongside current-loop local KV, it halves shared-stack decoding traversals relative to fixed 2-loop decoding. With parallel prefill, MoL-Hybrid decoding cuts fixed 2-loop latency by 3250% on S-size MoLT-KV and U-MoLT for 4,096-token prompts and 64 decoding steps, matching non-looped OLMo3 latency. We provide extensive empirical evidence and comprehensive ablations showing that MoLT consistently outperforms non-looped baselines across scales and architectures. In 400B-token pretraining against OLMo3 on 700M and 1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, U-MoLT reaches 1.7 token efficiency at 700M, while lowering 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and raising 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points on 3B MoE. In addition, in 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation reduces validation cross-entropy on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4 mean token efficiency.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Looped Transformers Sharing weights across depth goes back to Universal Transformers and ALBERT [15, 30]. Recent work scales looped language models across dense and MoE architectures [9, 19, 57, 71], varies loop depth through adaptive token routing or elastic compute budgets [2, 24], stabilizes deep unrolls [32, 44], and adapts pretrained models into looped backbones [8, 26, 35]. These approaches primarily carry computation across loops through the residual state. MoLT instead uses KV as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. As summarized in Table 1, it spans MoLT-R under loop residual, MoLT-KV under loop KV, and the encoderdecoder variant U-MoLT. Attention across depth Beyond standard residual connections, DenseFormer [42] aggregates earlier layer outputs with static weights, whereas Mixture-of-Depths Attention (MoDA) [70] and Attention Residuals [27] use input-dependent weights. In particular, MoDA jointly reads sequence KV and same-token depth KV within single pass. In looped architectures, CoTFormer, Dreamer, and RecurTrace expose intermediate representations across repeated computation [29, 38, 59]. In contrast, MoLA unifies cross-loop KV reuse and same-token depth attention within one attention distribution. Under loop residual, MoLT-R augments current-loop local KV with preceding-loop local KV at the same token position, allowing each layer to directly read intermediate representations from earlier layers in the current loop and all layers of the preceding loop. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV pairs current-loop local KV with strict-prefix memory KV from the preceding loop, separating same-token depth attention from cross-loop contextual feedback. Here, feedback refers to passing computed representations from one loop into the next. Prefix feedback and loop forcing Caching earlier hidden states across segments begins with same-level recurrence in Transformer-XL [13], whereas Staircase Attention and Feedback Transformer expose higher-level representations from earlier chunks or weighted layer mixture as memory for subsequent tokens [17, 25]. In non-looped Transformers, Layer-Condensed KV Cache (LCKV) shares top-layer KV across condensed layers under strict-prefix mask [62], and Recurrent Transformer attends to layer-output prefix KV alongside own-input KV within each layer [41]. Parallel iterative refinement has also been studied for latent thought tokens and hidden-state feedback [7, 16, 23, 58, 63, 67], whereas Deep Equilibrium Models solve for fixed points via root finding [3]. MoLT-KV introduces the loop KV paradigm for looped Transformers, pairing strict-prefix memory KV projected per layer from the preceding loops output with current-loop local KV at the current token. Through loop forcing, MoLT supervises next-token prediction at every loop from the initial memory-building pass onward, aligning cross-loop representations for recursive reuse beyond the training loop horizon. Combined with embedding restart and strict-prefix masking, this interface yields finite-prefix stabilization in token order without contraction assumptions or iterative root finding (Section B.1). KV sharing and efficient looped decoding Sharing KV caches reduces memory and computation in deep and looped Transformers. Cross-Layer Attention shares projected KV across adjacent layers [5], and recent looped models reduce KV overhead by updating shared cache, replaying selected loops, or sharing final-loop KV [12, 33, 45]. Looped Prediction Transformer (LPT) jointly attends to layers first-loop KV cache and current-loop sliding window, yet still relies on residual feedback and executes all loops sequentially per token [39]. Parallel Loop Transformer (PLT) reduces decoding latency by overlapping loops across token positions via shifted states [61], whereas LoopFold batches multiple loop depths for the same token prefix using predicted loop inputs and corrector [53]. Rather than executing or overlapping multiple loops per token, MoLT-KV and U-MoLT eliminate same-position cross-loop dependence through embedding restart and strict-prefix memory KV, unlocking single-traversal MoL decoding beyond the training loop horizon. Each new token reads cached prefix memory KV and appends its own memory KV in one traversal. MoL-Hybrid decoding further combines parallel fixed-loop prefill with this single-traversal decoding update, retaining prompt parallelism alongside reduced decoding cost and single persistent KV history for the shared stack. Decoder with encoder-sourced KV Separating memory construction from prediction readout reduces both KV storage and prefill computation. YOCO builds shared global KV cache in self-decoder and reuses it across cross-decoder [55], and Universal YOCO loops the self-decoder that constructs this cache [56]. sections.title: 3 Mixture-of-Loops Transformer
sections.content: Given tokens x0, . . . , xT 1, looped Transformer repeatedly applies shared network to produce representations for predicting xt+1 from xt. Each pass through the shared network is called loop. Passing computation from one loop into the next is referred to as cross-loop feedback, and we call subsequent loops after the first feedback loops. In the residual-feedback Loop Model, each loop passes its final state to the next. Its intermediate representations are not retained for direct reads in later loops, and each token remains dependent on its own preceding-loop state. We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), which uses KV as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops through Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) (Figs. 1 and 3). MoLT-R carries the preceding residual state forward and exposes retained local KV, while MoLT-KV restarts from embeddings and receives earlier-loop context through strict-prefix memory KV. Both are plain MoLT models: their shared loop stack has MoLA at every layer and feeds directly into the prediction head. U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT) separates 5 memory construction from prediction readout. Its MoLT Encoder uses loop KV to build feedback memory across loops, while its separate MoLT Decoder reads the encoder output to predict the next token. MoLT-R prioritizes expressivity, MoLT-KV brings single-traversal decoding to plain stack, and U-MoLT balances efficiency and quality through an encoderdecoder split, as compared in Section 5. We first define the feedback interfaces and the attention computation they support (Sections 3.1 and 3.2), separate memory construction from prediction readout (Section 3.3), and then present loop-forcing training and MoL decoding (Sections 3.4 and 3.5). In U-MoLT, each supervised loop runs the decoder and prediction head to compute its prediction loss. Each supervised loop trains its prediction path, and we compare loop-loss weights in Section 4.2. Loop forcing For MoLT-KV and U-MoLT, applying Eq. (8) with positive weight on every loop defines loop forcing. Analogous to teacher forcing, each feedback loop trains in parallel across tokens from the preceding loops strict-prefix memory KV rather than from sequentially decoded prefixes, reducing training from sequential steps to parallel passes. Allowing gradients through cross-loop feedback additionally lets later-loop losses refine the earlier computation that produces the feedback sources, while per-loop supervision remains applicable when cross-loop gradients are detached. After 2-loop training, single-traversal decoding achieves similar mean continuation CE to fixed 2-loop decoding on the evaluated windows (Section 4.4). Three design choices help support this shift to recursively generated prefix memory KV (Section B.2). Shared-readout supervision encourages the supervised loop outputs z1 and z2 to align. Embedding restart anchors each tokens residual stream to e(xt), while output and QK normalization keep activations and attention logits bounded.

sections.title: 3.5 Mixture-of-Loops Decoding
sections.content: We consider three decoding schedules: fixed-loop decoding, Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding, and MoLHybrid decoding. All MoLT variants support fixed-loop decoding, which preserves the chosen finite-loop computation. MoL decoding combines current-loop local KV with cached prefix memory KV and skips the preceding loops at each new token. In MoLT-KV and U-MoLT, embedding restart and strict-prefix loop KV feedback remove same-position cross-loop dependencies, enabling one traversal per decoding step. Both MoL decoding and MoL-Hybrid decoding use this single-traversal update, differing in how they initialize prompt memory KV. traversal executes the full Transformer backbone in plain MoLT or the encoder in U-MoLT once, over either the prompt or one token position, while decoder traversal executes the MoLT Decoder once over the requested positions. Prefill supplies the first continuation prediction, and each decoding step consumes one token to predict the next. Fixed-loop decoding Fixed-loop prefill executes traversals of the shared network, processing prompt positions in parallel within each loop. Fixed 2-loop decoding sets = 2. Each loop retains its own prefix sequence KV cache. During decoding, each new input token passes through all loops, reading and extending their respective caches before computing the final-loop prediction. MoLT-R also passes the current tokens normalized output and selected local KV from each loop to the next. These same-position sources require the tokens loops to execute in order. This preserves the chosen finite-loop computation and requires network traversals per decoding step. Mixture-of-Loops decoding Applied from empty caches, MoL decoding processes the prompt one token at time. At each position, one traversal starts from e(xt), jointly reads completed prefix memory KV at < and current-loop local KV through MoLA, and produces new output. Memory KV projected from the normalized output are appended to the cache for later tokens. Decoding uses the same update, so both phases require one traversal per token. MoL-Hybrid decoding MoL-Hybrid decoding combines fixed-loop parallel prefill with the MoL decoding update. MoL-Hybrid-1 and MoL-Hybrid-2 use 1-loop and 2-loop prefill, respectively, initializing prompt memory KV by projecting z1 and z2. In U-MoLT, decoder KV come from the final prefill loop. The prediction 10 at the final prefill position supplies the distribution for the first continuation token. Each decoding step uses one traversal and extends the retained caches, including memory KV projected from each new output. The history therefore combines finite-loop prompt caches with KV recursively appended during decoding, trading exact equivalence to an empty-cache sweep for parallel prompt processing. Key properties and inference costs Because embedding restart and strict-prefix memory reads at < remove same-position cross-loop dependence, every feedback loop reduces to strictly triangular recurrence across token positions. Position 0 has an empty prefix and stabilizes by loop 2 from any initial state, and each subsequent position stabilizes one loop after its prefix (Section B.1). Empty-cache MoL decoding therefore reaches the unique stabilized solution matched by every unroll of depth + 2. After length-P prompt, MoL-Hybrid decoding preserves the same cross-token recursion over continuation positions = 0, matching any multi-loop unroll that holds the prompt fixed and updates only the continuation for + 2 loops. Although each token traverses the shared stack once during decoding, recursive prefix memory propagation, current-loop depth KV, and U-MoLTs separate decoder preserve multi-loop prefix computation rather than collapsing to single-loop depth. Even with an equal split LE = LD = L/2, U-MoLT reaches at least 3L/2 blocks of causal path depth over earlier tokens, compared with at most in non-looped L-layer Transformer. Together, U-MoLT and loop KV close the inference efficiency gap in two steps. First, even under fixed 2-loop execution, omitting unused decoder traversals lets equal-split U-MoLT match non-looped L-layer Transformer in full-prompt prefill block depth (2LE = L) and quadratic prefill attention, while keeping decoding traversals and persistent KV storage at 1.5 instead of 2. Second, switching to MoL or MoL-Hybrid decoding lowers both an L-layer MoLT-KV stack and any U-MoLT partition with LE + LD = to block traversals per decoding step and single persistent prefix KV history for the shared stack, matching non-looped L-layer Transformer in total persistent KV storage. Under MoL-Hybrid-2, equal-split U-MoLT therefore matches non-looped backbone across all four dominant inference costs while retaining parallel prefill. Its remaining decoding overhead consists of LE extra memory KV projections and small depth attention, which scales as an O(LE/T ) fraction of sequence attention under full history. During 2-loop prefill, it also adds the single-position decoder readout at 1, prompt decoder KV projections, and extra memory KV projections. Section provides the formal proofs, loop-forcing alignment analysis, and complete traversal, KV-storage, and computational cost breakdowns for the all-layer loop KV architectures, and Section 4.4 evaluates these schedules empirically.

sections.title: 4.2 Component Ablations
sections.content: We study how feedback, depth sources, and decoder design affect model quality under common training protocol. Table 2 compares 32 S-size configurations in four blocks: OLMo3 Baseline, MoLT-R, MoLT-KV, and U-MoLT. All models are trained on 3B input tokens in BF16 with Muon, using seed 11 and the same parameter initialization. Two-loop models use equal loop-loss weights, i.e., 1:1. We report final-loop CE, update time, and parameter and FLOP differences relative to the baseline with the same loop count: method (1) for 1 loop and method (2) for 2 loops. The first three blocks in Table 2 use complete 12-layer stacks, while U-MoLT splits the stack into 6-layer encoder and 6-layer decoder. The depth-source choices progressively expand same-token local KV access: cur. layer reads the current layer, layer adds cross-layer sources in the current loop, and loop further adds cross-loop sources. For MoLT-KV and U-MoLT, loop is an extended ablation beyond the current-loop default in Section 3.2. Conversely, for MoLT-R, layer ablates the preceding-loop local KV reads included in Sections 3.1 and 3.2. Modern LLMs [28] often use hybrid architectures that mix full attention with linear or sparse attention layers. To test partial placement, we compare dense placement, which applies MoLA (or strict-prefix KV feedback in no-depth controls) at every layer, with sparse placement, which applies it at alternating layers while retaining ordinary causal self-attention at the remaining layers. For U-MoLT, self constructs decoder KV from each layers own hidden states, while shared and re-proj. read the encoder output through shared and independent per-layer KV projections, respectively, with re-proj. and current-loop layer corresponding to the Section 3.3 U-MoLT design. Looping and depth reuse improve prediction Residual looping improves prediction with unchanged parameter count. Moving from the single-loop method (1) to the 2-loop method (2) lowers CE from 3.318 to 3.299, gain of 0.019 at the same input-token budget. Both models have 112.972M parameters. The 2-loop recipe doubles logical training FLOPs and increases update time from 494 to 942 ms. Direct depth access further strengthens residual feedback. With dense placement, method (3) adds current-loop cross-layer sources to method (2) and lowers CE by 0.006. Method (5) further adds preceding-loop sources and improves on method (2) by 0.015. The preceding-loop gain also holds with sparse placement, where method (6) improves on method (2) by 0.013. Adding depth KV therefore lowers the best MoLT-R CE to 3.284 without adding parameters. Expanding depth KV sources also improves MoLT-KV under both placements. Without depth KV, methods (7) and (8) reduce feedback layers to strict-prefix cross-attention that cannot read KV at the current position. Both perform worse than the 2-loop baseline (2), and dense method (7) even performs worse than the single-loop baseline (1). CE decreases steadily from no depth to current-layer, cross-layer, and cross-loop access. Adding own KV provides direct same-position attention path alongside strict-prefix memory KV, complementing the residual and FFN paths. Reading earlier layers and the preceding loop brings further gains without adding parameters. In Table 2, no-depth methods (7) and (8) show 0.00% FLOPs because loop 2 projects only memory KV in place of local KV, whereas adding own KV computes both projections in loop 2 (+1.36% dense, +0.68% sparse) and expanding further to layer or loop reuses those local KV with negligible extra attention FLOPs. Placement depends on the feedback form Dense placement gives the best MoLT-R quality, while sparse placement gives MoLT-KV both lower CE and faster updates in all 4 source conditions. For MoLT-KV, sparse placement reduces CE by 0.0110.012 relative to dense placement and saves 1.770M parameters. Comparing the two feedback forms, MoLT-R outperforms MoLT-KV with dense cross-loop sources, while MoLT-KV outperforms MoLT-R with sparse cross-layer sources. These results make feedback form and placement joint design choice, with sparse KV feedback retaining ordinary self-attention between feedback layers. Independent decoder KV projections improve U-MoLT The U-shaped design allows decoder KV sources and projections to be chosen separately from encoder feedback. With ordinary decoder self-attention, moving from full-stack MoLT-KV to 6+6 split improves all 3 dense source conditions but raises CE in their sparse counterparts. sections.title: 4.5 Adapting Qwen through Continued Pretraining
sections.content: We test whether the MoLT feedback interface improves an existing pretrained backbone through matched continued pretraining (CT). Starting from Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, we train Qwen3.5-CT, U-MoLT-CT1, and U-MoLT-CT2 on the same 100B-token stream with the same tokenizer and AdamW schedule. Training uses 1.05M-token global batch and peak learning rate of 104, with 1.05B-token warmup and cosine decay to 105. Qwen3.5-CT retains the original architecture, while U-MoLT-CT1 and U-MoLT-CT2 apply two MoLT adaptations. Evaluation uses fixed validation blocks from 11 domains and their mean CE, with final second-loop predictions for the adaptations. Table 8 compares the three architectures after 100B tokens of continued pretraining. U-MoLT-CT1 and U-MoLT-CT2 differ in the source used to construct decoder Gated DeltaNet (GDN) [65] memory. Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base has 24 layers, comprising 18 GDN layers and 6 full-attention layers. Both adaptations split this backbone into 12-layer encoder and 12-layer decoder, with 9 GDN layers and 3 full-attention layers in each half. In the encoder, the 3 full-attention layers act as MoLA feedback layers reading strict-prefix memory KV from the preceding loop, while the 9 GDN layers remain recurrent sequence layers whose states reset between loops. Both use the re-proj. decoder-attention design in Table 2, with independent decoder KV projections at each attention layer. U-MoLT-CT1 constructs memory in the 9 decoder GDN layers from each layers own input, following the self source choice. Because these decoder GDN layers retain dependence on earlier decoder states, U-MoLT-CT1 is not strictly cross-only like pure-attention U-MoLT. U-MoLT-CT2 instead projects decoder GDN KV, decay gates, and update strengths from the normalized encoder output, while keeping queries and output gates dependent on the decoder state. Because 18 each Qwen3.5 GDN layer applies length-4 causal convolution to its queries, U-MoLT-CT2 still retains short-range cross-position decoder dependence across its 9 decoder GDN layers (a 28-token trailing window) rather than exact single-position prefill omission. The two adaptations share initialization, parameter count, encoder computation, and equal loop-loss weights. MoLT improves all 11 domains over the matched baseline Both adaptations achieve lower CE than Qwen3.5CT in every validation domain after 100B tokens. U-MoLT-CT1 reduces the equal-domain mean from 2.496 to 2.480, and U-MoLT-CT2 reaches 2.483  (Table 8)  . These broad improvements show that loop feedback transfers to an existing pretrained backbone under the same input-token budget, using additional shared-weight loop computation. Retaining decoder-state GDN writes gives the strongest adaptation. U-MoLT-CT1 outperforms U-MoLT-CT2 in all 11 domains, with mean CE advantage of 0.003. U-MoLT-CT1 reaches the baseline endpoint with fewer input tokens U-MoLT-CT1 matches Qwen3.5-CTs final domain-level CE after 66.378.3B input tokens along the recorded training trajectories  (Fig. 5)  . Across the 11 domains, this yields 1.281.51 input-token speedup, or 1.4 on average. These matching points are measured along the full 100B-token learning-rate schedule. The adaptations add only 3.15M parameters, increasing the language backbone from 752.39M to 755.54M, or 0.42%. With this small parameter overhead, loop reuse consistently improves the pretrained model across all 11 domains.

sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: Choosing among MoLT family architectures MoLT-R, MoLT-KV, and U-MoLT target distinct regimes across expressivity, efficiency, and backbone structure. Table 9 summarizes their mechanisms, inference profiles, and intended use cases. MoLT-R prioritizes expressivity over single-traversal inference. It keeps the residual stream across loops instead of passing earlier loops only through the normalized loop output. Without adding parameters, MoLA directly reads current-loop and preceding-loop local KV at the same token position. In Tables 4 and 5, MoLT-R reaches the highest 700M aggregate scores, with 59.2% mean 10-task accuracy and 14.84 mean 10-domain PPL. It also achieves the lowest validation CE among plain 12-layer stacks in Table 2. Our preliminary observations further indicate that its gain over plain residual feedback grows with effective computational depth, where information dilution in single residual stream becomes more severe. MoLT-R therefore fits expressivity-critical settings that can afford fixed -loop decoding and sequence KV caches. MoLT-KV prioritizes decoding efficiency with minimal architectural inductive bias. Embedding restart and strict-prefix memory KV remove same-position cross-loop dependence. Each decoding token can then skip preceding-loop traversals and run one traversal of the shared stack under MoL decoding. Relative to fixed -loop decoding, this cuts per-step decoding traversals and persistent KV storage by factor of . At = 2, MoL-Hybrid decoding reduces total S-size MoLT-KV latency by nearly half in Tables 6 and 7. Meanwhile, reading cached prefix memory KV across the shared L-layer stack preserves multi-loop computation over the prefix, as analyzed in Section B.1. Because MoL-Hybrid-2 still runs 2L full-prompt prefill blocks in MoLT-KV, this variant fits generation-heavy workloads where decoding dominates latency, matching U-MoLTs decoding speed. It also fits standard or hybrid backbones where additional architectural inductive bias is undesired. U-MoLT builds on loop KV by adding an architectural inductive bias tailored to autoregressive language modeling. It separates memory construction in looped MoLT Encoder from prediction readout in causal, cross-only MoLT Decoder. By Proposition 2, U-MoLT omits unused decoder traversals during prefill and intermediate loops. With an equal split LE = LD = L/2, MoL-Hybrid-2 removes the 2 prefill block depth of MoLT-KV. As shown in Section B.3, it matches non-looped L-layer backbone in full-prompt prefill block depth, quadratic prefill attention, decoding traversals, and persistent KV storage. With independent decoder KV projections, U-MoLT also lowers validation CE relative to MoLT-KV across all matched settings in Table 2. U-MoLT is therefore our default choice for general-purpose pure-attention language models. 19 Table 9 Quick-reference comparison of the three MoLT variants. We attribute this gain to decoupling two conflicting In standard stack, deep layers near the prediction head face two roles in deep autoregressive layers. competing pressures. First, for prediction, hidden states near the output must progressively collapse toward the next-token distribution p(xt+1 xt). This process discards or rewrites fine-grained semantic details of the current token. Second, for memory, self-attention KV are projected directly from each layers hidden states. Those same deep layers must therefore preserve clean historical context for future tokens at > t. MoLT-KV sharpens this conflict because its normalized loop output zr feeds the vocabulary projection while also supplying memory KV to the next loop. U-MoLT physically isolates these two responsibilities. The normalized encoder output zr sits midway through the network rather than directly beneath the prediction head. It can therefore act as high-fidelity shared memory without collapsing toward next-token logits. In contrast, hidden states in the cross-only MoLT Decoder never supply KV for future tokens and never feed back into the encoder. The decoder residual stream can therefore specialize toward predicting xt+1 without contaminating the memory read by later tokens. Even at the deepest decoder layers, independent decoder KV projections can still read clean context from zr right before the final prediction. Our ablations in Table 2 are consistent with this view. Across all 6 matched U-MoLT triplets, decoder self-attention under the self setting raises CE by 0.0140.021 relative to independent per-layer projections under re-proj. Independent projections also beat shared projections by 0.0090.018 CE, showing that decoder layers benefit from separate views of the same normalized encoder output. In Table 8, however, this cross-only decoder design also depends on the backbones sequence layers. On Qwen3.5, forcing decoder GDN layers to read only encoder-projected memory in U-MoLT-CT2 lags U-MoLT-CT1 by 0.003 mean CE across the 11 domains, while still not achieving exact single-position prefill omission (Section 4.5). On hybrid backbones with non-attention sequence mixers, retaining decoder-state recurrence in hybrid U-MoLT adaptations or using plain MoLT stacks therefore remains an important alternative. Beyond two stages: EncoderNeckDecoder architectures U-MoLT splits looped Transformer into two stages, using looped encoder for memory construction and cross-only decoder for prediction readout. natural generalization is three-stage EncoderNeckDecoder architecture. In this layout, non-looped encoder extracts foundational context, looped middle neck performs iterative cross-loop refinement, and cross-only decoder handles prediction readout. Informally, this forms giraffe network whose recurrent depth is elongated in the middle neck while keeping the encoder and decoder non-looped. In our preliminary experiments extending U-MoLT to this three-stage layout, looping the middle neck achieved the strongest validation results. This points toward an even cleaner separation among input encoding, iterative refinement, and prediction readout. We leave systematic study of this giraffe architecture, including stage partitioning and inference schedules, to future work. 20 Scaling to larger models Computational constraints have limited our scaling experiments to 700M and 1.5B dense models and 3B MoE models. How the gains from loop reuse evolve with larger model capacity and training budgets remains an open question. broader scaling study could compare allocating additional computation to larger models or to additional loops, measuring prediction quality alongside training and inference cost. Such experiments would help determine how to balance parameter capacity and shared-weight loop computation as MoLT scales up.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we present Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), which uses keys and values (KV) as memory to selectively reuse computation across depths and loops. Through Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA), MoLT spans MoLT-R under loop residual for expressivity and MoLT-KV under loop KV for plain-stack efficiency. Under loop KV, embedding restart and strict-prefix memory KV remove same-position cross-loop dependence. Trained via loop forcing, this enables single-traversal MoL decoding beyond the training loop horizon, while MoL-Hybrid decoding adds parallel prefill. To balance efficiency and quality, U-MoLT further separates memory construction from prediction readout and omits unused decoder traversals at inference. Experiments on 700M and 1.5B dense models and 3B MoE models trained with the OLMo3 recipe show consistent gains in perplexity and downstream accuracy. Continued pretraining on Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base confirms effective transfer to pretrained backbones, and MoL-Hybrid decoding achieves substantial latency reductions over fixed-loop decoding. These results suggest that explicit KV reuse across depths and loops is practical and effective primitive for scaling computational depth in looped Transformers. We will release the full implementation of MoLT, and we hope it will serve as foundation for building stronger looped large language models in the open-source community. MoLT integrates naturally with dense, MoE, and hybrid backbones. Beyond language modeling, it can be readily extended to multimodal intelligence, visual understanding, and world models, where iterative Transformer computation is increasingly adopted. We believe that principled information reuse across depths and loops will bring broad and lasting benefits across these diverse domains.

Three training and architectural choices help support this shift in memory source. First, supervising next-token prediction at every loop through the shared prediction readout encourages z1 and z2 to align under 2-loop training. In MoLT-KV, the shared vocabulary projection maps each supervised zr directly to next-token logits. In U-MoLT, the shared cross-only decoder starts from r,LE and reads zr through independent decoder KV projections across all LD layers. Both loops also run the same shared stack from e(xt). With open gradients, later-loop losses also backpropagate into z1 through memory KV. Positive loop-1 weight then prevents later-loop losses from reshaping z1 solely as an internal feedback source. Because sequence length typically far exceeds encoder depth, full-history depth attention accounts for only an O(LE/T ) fraction of sequence attention in both full-sequence loops and single-token decoding. This explains why expanding depth access from own KV to full history adds negligible attention FLOPs in Table 2. Keeping MoLA within the LE-layer encoder in U-MoLT reduces this O(L2 E) term further. In U-MoLT, Proposition 2 also removes quadratic prefill attention in the decoder. Running the decoder only at position 1 lowers prefill decoder attention from O(LDP 2Hqh) to O(LDP Hqh). With an equal split LE = LD = L/2, 2-loop prefill in U-MoLT matches non-looped L-layer Transformer in quadratic prefill attention, whereas MoL-Hybrid-1 cuts it in half. Together, these bounds show how U-MoLT and loop KV close the inference efficiency gap in two steps. First, even under fixed 2-loop execution, Proposition 2 lets equal-split U-MoLT match non-looped full-prompt block depth and quadratic prefill attention. It also keeps decoding traversals and persistent KV storage at 1.5 instead of 2, while reaching 3L/2 blocks of prefix path depth. Second, MoL and MoL-Hybrid decoding avoid repeating the shared stack at each step and avoid separate per-loop prefix KV caches. Both architectures therefore run decoding blocks per step with one persistent prefix KV history for the shared stack. Under MoL-Hybrid-2, equal-split U-MoLT matches non-looped L-layer Transformer across all four dominant costs while keeping parallel prefill. Its remaining decoding overhead is small depth attention and LE extra memory KV projections, while 2-loop prefill adds the decoder readout at 1, prompt decoder KV projections, and extra memory KV projections. Sparse feedback placement keeps the same persistent KV storage by retaining one current-loop sequence KV cache per non-feedback layer.
